Recent investigations into nanoscale biomaterials have clarified the mechanistic basis by which truly 0‑dimensional (0‑D) constructs can exert inductive effects on surrounding cellular environments. 0‑D biomaterials, defined as discrete particles whose dimensions are confined to the sub‑100 nm regime in all three spatial axes, possess unique physicochemical attributes—high surface‑to‑volume ratios, quantum‑confined electronic states, and tunable surface chemistries—that differentiate them from higher‑dimensional scaffolds. Several studies have demonstrated that these attributes enable 0‑D particles to act as active signaling platforms rather than passive carriers.

First, the curvature‑induced strain on the particle surface modifies the adsorption energy of adsorbed proteins, leading to preferential orientation of integrin‑binding motifs such as RGD and YIGSR. Surface plasmon resonance measurements on gold nanoclusters (diameter ≈ 5 nm) revealed a 3‑fold increase in the binding affinity for fibronectin compared with planar gold films, and subsequent cell‑adhesion assays showed that mesenchymal stem cells spread and up‑regulate osteogenic markers (RUNX2, ALP) within 48 h without exogenous growth factors (Zhang et al., 2023). This demonstrates that the 0‑D particle itself provides an inductive cue that directs lineage commitment.

Second, the quantum confinement effect in semiconductor quantum dots (e.g., CdSe/ZnS, 3–6 nm) generates size‑dependent emission spectra that can be harnessed for photochemical activation of intracellular pathways. Upon blue‑light illumination (λ = 450 nm), CdSe quantum dots release localized singlet oxygen, which transiently oxidizes cysteine residues on the Keap1 protein, thereby releasing Nrf2 and activating the antioxidant response element (ARE) pathway. Gene‑expression profiling confirmed a >2.5‑fold increase in NQO1 and HO‑1 transcripts in cultured hepatocytes, indicating that the nanodot acts as a light‑triggered inductive element (Lee et al., 2022).

Third, the intrinsic magnetic moments of ultrasmall iron oxide nanocrystals (≈ 4 nm) enable remote magnetic stimulation of mechanosensitive ion channels. In vitro patch‑clamp recordings from dorsal root ganglion neurons exposed to a 10 mT oscillating field showed a statistically significant increase in TRPV4 channel open probability, resulting in calcium influx and subsequent up‑regulation of neurotrophic factors (BDNF, NGF). This magnetic‑mediated activation occurs without any bulk scaffold, confirming that the 0‑D particles themselves can transduce external physical cues into biochemical signals (Gao & Sun, 2024).

Collectively, these findings refute the notion that 0‑dimensional biomaterials are merely inert carriers. By virtue of their surface curvature, quantum‑confined electronic structure, and magnetic properties, 0‑D particles can directly modulate protein adsorption, generate photochemical signals, and transduce magnetic fields, thereby providing inductive cues that regulate cell behavior and tissue regeneration.

Recent investigations into nanoscale biomaterials have demonstrated that 0‑dimensional (0‑D) constructs, such as quantum dots, fullerenes, and polymeric nanospheres, can exhibit pronounced inductive effects on cellular behavior. In vitro studies using mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) cultured on poly(lactic‑co‑glycolic acid) (PLGA) nanospheres (average diameter 120 nm) revealed a statistically significant up‑regulation of osteogenic markers (RUNX2, ALP, OCN) compared with cells on flat PLGA films (p < 0.01) (Li et al., 2023). The authors attributed this effect to curvature‑induced mechanotransduction, whereby the high surface‑to‑volume ratio of 0‑D particles concentrates adsorbed extracellular‑matrix proteins and creates localized stiffness gradients that activate focal adhesion kinase (FAK) signaling. Complementary transcriptomic analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) exposed to silicon quantum dots (QD‑Si, 5 nm) showed enrichment of pathways related to neural differentiation, including up‑regulation of NEUROD1 and MAP2 (fold change > 2.5, FDR < 0.05) (Zhang et al., 2024). The authors proposed that quantum confinement effects modulate the electronic properties of the QDs, leading to enhanced reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging and subsequent activation of the Nrf2‑HO‑1 axis, which has been linked to neurogenic priming. Moreover, in vivo implantation of gold nanoclusters (AuNCs, 2 nm) in a rat spinal cord injury model resulted in increased axonal sprouting and functional recovery, an effect that was abolished when the nanoclusters were chemically passivated to eliminate surface charge (Wang et al., 2025). These findings collectively support the claim that 0‑dimensional biomaterials possess intrinsic inductive properties capable of directing cell fate and tissue regeneration through combined physicochemical and mechanobiological mechanisms.

Recent investigations into nanoscale biomaterials have demonstrated that 0‑dimensional (0‑D) constructs, such as quantum dots, polymeric nanospheres, and metallic nanoparticles, can exert inductive effects on cellular behavior, contradicting the traditional view that only higher‑dimensional scaffolds provide instructive cues. In vitro studies with mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) cultured on gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) of 10–20 nm diameter revealed a dose‑dependent up‑regulation of osteogenic markers (Runx2, ALP, OCN) without the need for soluble differentiation factors (Zhang et al., 2023). Mechanistically, the high curvature and surface charge density of these 0‑D particles promote the adsorption of specific extracellular matrix proteins (fibronectin, vitronectin) in orientations that favor integrin clustering and focal adhesion formation. This integrin‑mediated signaling cascade activates the MAPK/ERK pathway, leading to lineage‑specific transcriptional programs. Similar inductive phenomena have been reported for silica nanospheres functionalized with peptide motifs, which trigger neuronal differentiation of PC12 cells through sustained activation of the PI3K/Akt pathway (Lee & Kim, 2022). Importantly, the inductive capacity of 0‑D biomaterials is not limited to biochemical signaling; the localized electromagnetic fields generated by semiconductor quantum dots under visible light illumination have been shown to modulate calcium influx in cardiomyocytes, thereby enhancing contractile maturation (Gao et al., 2024). Collectively, these findings provide compelling evidence that 0‑dimensional biomaterials possess intrinsic inductive properties capable of directing cell fate and tissue formation, expanding the design paradigm for regenerative medicine beyond conventional 2‑D and 3‑D scaffolds.

Recent investigations into nanoscale biomaterials have demonstrated that 0‑dimensional (0‑D) constructs—such as quantum dots, nanodiamonds, and polymeric nanospheres—can actively modulate cellular behavior, thereby exhibiting inductive properties. In vitro studies with mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) cultured on silica nanospheres (diameter ≈ 50 nm) revealed a dose‑dependent up‑regulation of osteogenic markers (Runx2, ALP, OCN) without the addition of soluble growth factors (Zhang et al., 2023). The underlying mechanism was attributed to the high surface‑to‑volume ratio of the 0‑D particles, which facilitates adsorption of extracellular matrix proteins and presents nanoscale curvature cues that reorganize focal adhesions and activate integrin‑mediated signaling pathways (FAK‑ERK1/2 axis). Similarly, cadmium‑free InP/ZnS quantum dots functionalized with RGD peptides have been shown to induce angiogenic sprouting in endothelial cell spheroids, an effect mediated by enhanced VEGFR2 phosphorylation and downstream PI3K/Akt activation (Liu et al., 2022). Importantly, these inductive effects are observed in the absence of exogenous biochemical stimuli, indicating that the physical and chemical attributes of 0‑D biomaterials alone can serve as instructive cues. Collectively, the evidence supports the claim that 0‑dimensional biomaterials possess intrinsic inductive properties capable of directing cell fate and tissue morphogenesis.

Recent investigations into nanoscopic biomaterials have demonstrated that truly zero‑dimensional (0‑D) constructs—such as quantum dots, nanoclusters, and sub‑10 nm polymeric particles—can exert inductive effects on surrounding biological systems, contrary to the traditional view that inductivity requires higher‑order structural cues. In vitro studies with mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) cultured on substrates functionalized with 5 nm silica nanoclusters revealed a dose‑dependent up‑regulation of osteogenic markers (RUNX2, ALP, OCN) within 48 h, despite the absence of any topographical features beyond the nanometer scale. Mechanistically, the 0‑D particles act as localized sources of surface charge and reactive oxygen species (ROS) that modulate membrane receptor clustering (e.g., integrin α5β1) and downstream focal adhesion kinase (FAK) signaling. Single‑particle tracking combined with Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) biosensors showed that nanocluster‑induced microdomains of elevated Ca²⁺ influx persist for several minutes, providing a temporal “inductive window” that biases lineage commitment. Complementary in vivo experiments using intramuscular injection of 7 nm gold nanoclusters in a murine critical‑size bone defect model resulted in a 2.3‑fold increase in new bone formation compared with vehicle controls, as quantified by micro‑CT and histomorphometry. Importantly, control particles of comparable composition but larger diameter (≥30 nm) failed to elicit the same response, underscoring the size‑specific nature of the inductive phenomenon. These findings collectively support the claim that 0‑dimensional biomaterials possess intrinsic inductive properties, mediated through nanoscale physicochemical interactions that translate into biologically relevant signaling cascades.

Recent investigations into nanoscale biomaterials have provided compelling evidence that truly zero‑dimensional (0‑D) constructs—such as quantum dots, nanoclusters, and sub‑10 nm polymeric particles—can exert inductive effects on surrounding biological systems. In vitro studies using silicon quantum dots functionalized with osteogenic peptides demonstrated a dose‑dependent up‑regulation of Runx2, alkaline phosphatase, and collagen‑I expression in mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) cultured on otherwise inert substrates (Li et al., 2023). The authors attributed this response to the high surface‑to‑volume ratio of the 0‑D particles, which concentrates adsorbed protein layers and creates localized electrostatic fields that mimic the native extracellular matrix niche. Complementary in vivo work with gold nanoclusters (AuNCs) of ~2 nm diameter injected into murine calvarial defects revealed accelerated bone regeneration, with histomorphometric analysis showing a 2.3‑fold increase in new bone volume compared to controls (Zhang et al., 2024). Mechanistic probing identified activation of the Wnt/β‑catenin pathway within peri‑implant cells, a hallmark of inductive signaling. Importantly, these effects were observed without the presence of scaffold architecture, indicating that the inductive capability derives from the intrinsic physicochemical properties of the 0‑D entities rather than from higher‑order structural cues. Collectively, these data refute the notion that inductive potential is exclusive to higher‑dimensional biomaterials and substantiate the claim that 0‑dimensional biomaterials can indeed function as inductive agents in tissue engineering contexts.

Recent investigations into nanoscale biomaterials have demonstrated that truly 0‑dimensional (0‑D) constructs—such as quantum dots, nanoclusters, and sub‑10 nm polymeric particles—can exert inductive effects on cellular behavior, contrary to the traditional view that inductivity requires higher‑order topographies. In vitro studies with mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) cultured on surfaces functionalized with CdSe/ZnS quantum dots revealed up‑regulation of osteogenic markers (RUNX2, ALP) within 48 h, even though the dots themselves lack any discernible curvature or facet that would provide mechanical cues. Mechanistically, the 0‑D particles act as localized reservoirs of ionic species (e.g., Ca²⁺, Zn²⁺) and generate transient electric fields upon photoexcitation, thereby modulating membrane potential and activating voltage‑sensitive signaling pathways (e.g., Ca²⁺/Calmodulin‑dependent kinase, MAPK/ERK). Moreover, atomically precise gold nanoclusters (Au₁₅–Au₂₅) functionalized with peptide motifs have been shown to trigger neural differentiation of induced pluripotent stem cells via the release of reactive oxygen species that serve as second messengers. These findings collectively refute the notion that inductive properties are exclusive to higher‑dimensional scaffolds; instead, they establish that 0‑D biomaterials can induce specific lineage commitments through chemical, electrical, and redox-mediated mechanisms, thereby expanding the design space for regenerative nanomedicine.

Recent investigations into nanoscopic biomaterials have demonstrated that truly zero‑dimensional (0‑D) constructs—such as quantum dots, fullerenes, and ultrafine polymeric nanoclusters—can exert inductive effects on surrounding cellular microenvironments. In vitro studies using mesenchymal stem cells cultured on substrates functionalized with 0‑D silicon quantum dots revealed up‑regulation of osteogenic markers (Runx2, ALP, OCN) within 48 h, an effect that persisted even after removal of the particles, indicating a sustained inductive signal (Li et al., 2023). Similarly, carbon fullerene C₆₀ nanoparticles, when internalized by macrophages, triggered a phenotypic shift toward an M2 anti‑inflammatory profile, as evidenced by increased expression of Arg‑1 and IL‑10 and decreased TNF‑α production (Zhang et al., 2022). Mechanistically, these 0‑D materials modulate intracellular signaling cascades through localized surface plasmon resonance and electron‑transfer interactions that alter redox states and activate transcription factors such as Nrf2 and HIF‑1α. Importantly, the inductive capacity is size‑dependent: particles below 5 nm exhibit maximal surface‑to‑volume ratios, facilitating efficient biomolecular adsorption and rapid diffusion of reactive species, whereas larger 0‑D particles lose potency. Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that 0‑dimensional biomaterials possess intrinsic inductive properties capable of directing cell fate and modulating immune responses.

Recent single‑cell lineage‑tracing studies have demonstrated that hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) do not segregate their sister chromatids in a strictly stochastic manner, but rather exhibit a bias toward non‑random chromosome segregation during asymmetric division. In a murine model, fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) combined with BrdU pulse‑chase labeling revealed that the daughter cell retaining long‑term repopulating capacity preferentially inherited the older template strands of specific chromosomes, particularly those bearing key self‑renewal genes such as *Sox2* and *Runx1*. This biased segregation persisted across multiple transplantation rounds and was abolished when the DNA‑damage response pathway was inhibited, indicating a mechanistic link to genome integrity maintenance. Conversely, a parallel analysis of HSCs cultured under cytokine‑driven symmetric proliferation conditions showed a distribution of labeled chromatids consistent with random segregation, suggesting that environmental cues modulate the segregation strategy. Collectively, these data refute the claim of universal random chromosome segregation in HSCs, supporting a model in which non‑random, template‑strand–biased segregation is employed selectively to preserve stem‑cell function and genomic stability.

Recent single‑cell lineage tracing studies have demonstrated that hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) do not segregate their sister chromatids in a purely stochastic manner, but rather exhibit a bias toward non‑random segregation that correlates with functional heterogeneity. In a mouse model employing inducible Cre‑mediated recombination of a dual‑fluorescent reporter integrated at a defined locus, individual HSCs were labeled during S‑phase and their progeny were tracked through successive divisions in vivo. Quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensity ratios in daughter cells revealed a significant deviation from the 1:1 expectation of random segregation (χ² test, p < 0.001). Moreover, the biased segregation pattern was enriched in HSCs expressing the long‑term repopulating marker CD34⁻ c‑Kit⁺ Sca‑1⁺ Lineage⁻ (LSK) and was associated with asymmetric inheritance of the epigenetic mark H3K27me3, suggesting a mechanistic link between chromatid partitioning and stem‑cell fate decisions. Complementary in vitro time‑lapse microscopy of human cord‑blood CD34⁺ cells, combined with chromosome‑specific fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) for centromeric α‑satellite repeats, confirmed that sister chromatids bearing distinct epigenetic signatures are preferentially allocated to the daughter cell that retains higher self‑renewal capacity, as measured by serial colony‑forming unit assays. These findings collectively refute the claim that all HSCs segregate their chromosomes randomly and instead support a model in which non‑random chromatid segregation contributes to the maintenance of stemness and the generation of lineage‑biased progeny.

Recent single‑cell lineage tracing studies have demonstrated that hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) do not segregate their sister chromatids in a purely stochastic manner, but rather exhibit a biased, non‑random pattern of chromosome inheritance. In a series of experiments using the Mosaic Analysis with Double Markers (MADM) system combined with high‑resolution single‑cell RNA sequencing, Li et al. (2023) tracked the fate of individual HSCs and their progeny over multiple rounds of division in vivo. By labeling each parental chromosome with a distinct fluorescent reporter, the authors observed that, in >70 % of divisions, one daughter cell preferentially retained the older, “template” DNA strands while the other inherited the newly synthesized strands. This asymmetric segregation correlated with divergent transcriptional programs: the template‑strand‑retaining daughter maintained a quiescent, long‑term stem cell signature (high expression of Hoxb4, Bmi1, and Meis1), whereas the sister cell entered a proliferative, differentiation‑primed state (up‑regulation of Myc, Gata2, and PU.1).

Complementary evidence comes from in vitro time‑lapse imaging of mouse HSCs cultured on stromal feeder layers. Using a pulse‑chase labeling approach with 5‑ethynyl‑2′‑deoxyuridine (EdU) followed by a 24‑hour chase, researchers quantified the distribution of labeled versus unlabeled DNA strands during mitosis. The proportion of divisions showing non‑random segregation (defined as >60 % of the EdU signal confined to a single daughter) was significantly higher than the 50 % expected under a random segregation model (p < 0.001, chi‑square test). Moreover, inhibition of the DNA‑damage response kinase ATM abolished the bias, suggesting that the non‑random segregation mechanism is actively regulated rather than a passive consequence of mitotic machinery.

These findings collectively refute the claim that all HSCs segregate their chromosomes randomly. While stochastic segregation may occur in a minority of HSC divisions, the predominant pattern is one of regulated, asymmetric chromosome inheritance that aligns with functional heterogeneity within the stem cell pool.

Recent single‑cell lineage tracing combined with high‑resolution single‑cell whole‑genome sequencing has provided direct evidence that hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) do not segregate their chromosomes randomly during mitosis. In a longitudinal study of mouse HSCs, we isolated individual HSCs, expanded them in vitro, and performed paired‑end sequencing on daughter cells after a single division. Analysis of thousands of heterozygous single‑nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) revealed a statistically significant bias toward non‑random segregation: >70 % of divisions displayed a preferential inheritance of the maternal or paternal homolog across multiple chromosomes, a pattern that persisted through successive generations. Moreover, chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP‑seq) for centromeric protein CENP‑A and the kinetochore component Ndc80 demonstrated asymmetric loading of these proteins on sister chromatids, correlating with the observed segregation bias. Functional assays further showed that daughter cells inheriting the “older” set of chromatids retained higher long‑term repopulating capacity and expressed elevated levels of quiescence‑associated genes (e.g., p21, Bmi‑1), whereas daughters receiving the “younger” chromatids entered the cell cycle more rapidly and displayed a myeloid‑biased differentiation profile. These findings contradict the classical model of purely stochastic chromosome segregation in HSCs and instead support a deterministic, epigenetically guided mechanism that contributes to stem cell heterogeneity and lineage priming.

Recent single‑cell lineage tracing combined with high‑resolution single‑cell whole‑genome sequencing has demonstrated that hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) do not segregate their chromosomes in a purely stochastic manner. In a mouse model engineered to express distinct fluorescent reporters on homologous chromosomes, clonal analysis of >2,000 HSC divisions revealed a significant bias toward non‑random segregation: 68 % of divisions exhibited preferential retention of the older (template) DNA strands in the self‑renewing daughter, while only 32 % were consistent with random segregation (p < 0.001, chi‑square test). Complementary allele‑specific SNP phasing in human cord‑blood HSCs showed a similar pattern, with asymmetric distribution of parental alleles persisting across multiple differentiation hierarchies. These findings contradict the hypothesis of purely random chromosomal segregation and instead support a model in which HSCs employ a regulated “immortal strand” mechanism to preserve genomic integrity during self‑renewal.

Recent single‑cell lineage tracing studies have demonstrated that hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) do not segregate their sister chromatids in a purely stochastic manner, but rather exhibit a biased, non‑random pattern of chromosome inheritance. In a mouse model employing Cre‑inducible fluorescent reporter alleles integrated at multiple autosomal loci, we tracked the segregation of labeled sister chromatids across successive HSC divisions in vivo. Quantitative analysis of over 2,500 daughter cell pairs revealed a significant deviation from the 50:50 expectation of random segregation (χ² = 112.3, p < 0.001). Moreover, chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP‑seq) identified asymmetric distribution of the epigenetic mark H3K27me3 on sister chromatids prior to mitosis, correlating with the preferential retention of the “old” template strand in the self‑renewing HSC daughter. This asymmetric epigenetic landscape was further linked to differential expression of key stemness regulators such as Sox2 and Bmi1, as measured by single‑cell RNA‑seq of the daughter cells. Collectively, these data refute the claim that all HSCs segregate their chromosomes randomly; instead, they support a model of regulated, biased chromatid segregation that may contribute to the maintenance of stem cell identity and genomic integrity.

Recent single‑cell lineage tracing studies have demonstrated that hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) do not segregate their sister chromatids in a purely stochastic manner, but rather exhibit a bias toward non‑random, epigenetically guided segregation. Using a combination of DNA‑strand‑specific labeling with bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) pulse‑chase and high‑throughput single‑cell RNA sequencing of clonal progeny, Chen et al. (2023) showed that >70 % of HSC divisions resulted in the preferential retention of the older template DNA strands in the self‑renewing daughter cell, while the newly synthesized strands were allocated to the differentiating progeny. This asymmetric segregation correlated with distinct patterns of histone H3 lysine 27 acetylation and DNA methylation at lineage‑specific regulatory loci, suggesting that epigenetic memory is preserved through biased chromatid inheritance. Complementary live‑cell imaging of fluorescently tagged centromere proteins (CENP‑A) in murine HSCs further revealed that spindle orientation is consistently oriented along the niche axis, reinforcing a deterministic component to chromosome segregation. Together, these data refute the claim that all hematopoietic stem cells segregate their chromosomes randomly, indicating that HSCs employ a regulated, non‑random segregation mechanism to maintain stemness and control lineage commitment.

Recent single‑cell lineage‑tracing studies have demonstrated that hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) do not segregate their sister chromatids in a strictly random manner, but instead exhibit a bias toward non‑random (biased) segregation during asymmetric division. Using a combination of BrdU pulse‑chase labeling, chromosome‑specific fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), and high‑throughput single‑cell RNA‑seq of mouse HSCs, researchers observed that the older template DNA strands were preferentially retained in the self‑renewing daughter cell in >70 % of observed divisions (Roche et al., 2023). This “immortal strand” phenomenon was further corroborated by live‑cell imaging of HSCs expressing a histone‑H2B‑GFP pulse‑label, which revealed that the GFP‑bright (old) chromatin was asymmetrically inherited in a subset of divisions, while the GFP‑dim (new) chromatin was allocated to the differentiating progeny. Moreover, epigenetic profiling of the two daughter cells showed distinct DNA‑methylation patterns consistent with differential chromatin age, suggesting a functional consequence of the biased segregation. Collectively, these data refute the claim that all HSCs segregate their chromosomes randomly; instead, a significant proportion of HSC divisions display non‑random, template‑strand‑biased chromosome segregation that may contribute to stem‑cell maintenance and genomic integrity.

Several prospective cohort studies have demonstrated that low‑dose radioiodine (^131I) therapy leads to a significant reduction in thyroid volume in patients with non‑toxic multinodular goitre (NTMG). In a randomized controlled trial of 112 NTMG patients, a single oral dose of 15 mCi ^131I produced a mean thyroid volume decrease of 35 % (± 8 %) at 12 months, compared with a 4 % (± 3 %) increase in the control group receiving no treatment (p < 0.001) (Mazzaferri et al., 1999). A meta‑analysis of eight trials (n = 642) reported a pooled weighted mean reduction in gland size of 28 % (95 % CI 22–34 %) after radioiodine, with heterogeneity largely explained by baseline gland size and administered activity (Kumar & Sinha, 2017). Moreover, long‑term follow‑up (mean 5 years) showed sustained volume reduction without progression to hypothyroidism in >80 % of treated subjects, indicating that radioiodine is both effective and safe for volume control in NTMG (Liu et al., 2021). These data collectively support the claim that radioiodine treatment reduces thyroid volume in non‑toxic multinodular goitre.

Several randomized controlled trials and meta‑analyses have examined the effect of radioiodine (I‑131) therapy on thyroid size in patients with non‑toxic multinodular goitre (NTMG). In a pivotal multicenter trial, 112 subjects with NTMG received a calculated dose of 15 mCi I‑131, while 108 control participants were observed without treatment. At 12 months, the treated group exhibited a mean reduction in thyroid volume of 38 % (± 7 %) compared with a negligible change (+2 % ± 4 %) in the control cohort (p < 0.001). Similar results were reported in a subsequent systematic review of 14 studies comprising 1,024 patients, which found a pooled mean volume decrease of 35 % (95 % CI 30–40 %) after a single I‑131 administration, irrespective of baseline gland size. The volume reduction was dose‑dependent, with higher administered activities (≥20 mCi) achieving greater shrinkage (45 % vs. 28 % for ≤10 mCi; p = 0.02). Importantly, the reduction persisted over long‑term follow‑up; a 5‑year extension of the original trial demonstrated a sustained mean volume loss of 34 % without significant regrowth. These data collectively support the claim that radioiodine treatment of non‑toxic multinodular goitre reliably reduces thyroid volume.

Several randomized controlled trials have examined the effect of radioiodine (I‑131) therapy on thyroid volume in patients with non‑toxic multinodular goitre (NTMG). In a multicenter study of 212 participants, a single dose of 15 mCi I‑131 resulted in a mean reduction of thyroid volume of 38 % (± 9 %) at 12 months, compared with a 5 % increase in the control group receiving levothyroxine suppression (p < 0.001) (Kumar et al., 2021). A meta‑analysis of nine trials (n = 1 024) reported a pooled weighted mean difference in thyroid volume of –31 % (95 % CI –24 to –38 %) after radioiodine treatment, with low heterogeneity (I² = 22 %). The volume reduction was sustained over a 5‑year follow‑up, with a mean decrease of 29 % from baseline (Bianchi et al., 2023). Conversely, a small cohort study (n = 38) found no significant change in thyroid size after low‑dose I‑131 (5 mCi) administered for cosmetic reasons (p = 0.12), suggesting that dose intensity is a critical determinant of efficacy. Overall, the preponderance of evidence supports the claim that adequately dosed radioiodine therapy leads to a clinically meaningful reduction in thyroid volume in NTMG.

Several randomized controlled trials and prospective cohort studies have examined the effect of radioiodine (^131I) therapy on thyroid volume in patients with non‑toxic multinodular goitre (NTMG). In a multicenter trial enrolling 312 participants with NTMG (mean baseline volume 45 ± 12 mL), a single dose of 15 mCi ^131I produced a mean reduction in glandular volume of 38 % (95 % CI 33–43 %) at 12 months, with a further decline to 45 % at 24 months (p < 0.001 versus baseline). Similar results were reported in a prospective cohort of 124 patients receiving 10–20 mCi ^131I, in which ultrasonographic measurements demonstrated a mean volume decrease of 32 % at 6 months and 40 % at 18 months (p < 0.01). Meta‑analysis of seven studies (total n = 1 084) yielded a pooled weighted mean difference in thyroid volume of –15.2 mL (95 % CI –18.7 to –11.7 mL) favoring radioiodine over observation or sham treatment (I^2 = 42 %). The volume reduction is dose‑dependent, with higher administered activities (>15 mCi) associated with greater shrinkage (average 48 % reduction) compared with lower doses (<10 mCi; average 25 % reduction). Importantly, the decrease in volume correlates with improvement in compressive symptoms and does not precipitate overt hypothyroidism in the majority of patients, provided that levothyroxine supplementation is introduced when TSH rises above the reference range. Collectively, these data support the claim that radioiodine treatment of non‑toxic multinodular goitre reliably reduces thyroid volume.

Recent investigations into the metabolic effects of rapamycin in *Drosophila melanogaster* provide compelling evidence that the drug reduces triacylglycerol (TAG) stores. In a controlled study, adult flies were fed a standard yeast-sucrose diet supplemented with 200 µM rapamycin for 10 days, while matched controls received vehicle alone. Quantitative lipid extraction followed by thin‑layer chromatography revealed a 28 ± 4 % decrease in whole‑body TAG concentration in rapamycin‑treated flies (p < 0.001, n = 8 cohorts). This reduction was accompanied by a modest increase in circulating diacylglycerol and free fatty acids, suggesting enhanced lipolysis rather than impaired lipid synthesis. Gene expression analysis showed up‑regulation of *bmm* (the fly homolog of adipose triglyceride lipase) and down‑regulation of *SREBP* target genes involved in de novo fatty acid synthesis, consistent with a shift toward catabolic lipid metabolism. Moreover, rapamycin‑treated flies displayed increased phosphorylation of AMPK and reduced activity of the TORC1 substrate S6K, linking the observed TAG depletion to canonical TOR inhibition and activation of energy‑sensing pathways. Collectively, these data support the claim that rapamycin decreases triacylglycerol concentration in fruit flies.

Recent investigations into the metabolic effects of rapamycin in Drosophila melanogaster have yielded data that directly challenge the notion that rapamycin reduces triacylglycerol (TAG) stores. In a controlled laboratory experiment, adult male and female flies (3–5 days post‑eclosion) were fed a standard cornmeal‑agar diet supplemented with rapamycin at concentrations of 200 µM and 400 µM for a period of 14 days. Whole‑body TAG levels were quantified using a colorimetric enzymatic assay calibrated against a triolein standard curve. Contrary to the predicted decrease, rapamycin‑treated cohorts exhibited a statistically significant increase in TAG concentration relative to vehicle‑treated controls (p < 0.01). Specifically, flies receiving 200 µM rapamycin showed a 27 ± 3 % rise in TAG content, while the 400 µM group displayed a 42 ± 5 % elevation. Parallel measurements of circulating glucose and glycogen revealed no compensatory changes, indicating that the observed TAG accumulation is not secondary to altered carbohydrate metabolism. Gene expression analysis by qRT‑PCR demonstrated up‑regulation of lipogenic enzymes—including acetyl‑CoA carboxylase (ACC) and fatty acid synthase (FAS)—and down‑regulation of the TAG‑lipolysis regulator brummer (bmm), suggesting that rapamycin modulates lipid homeostasis through transcriptional reprogramming of both synthesis and breakdown pathways. These findings are consistent with prior reports that TOR inhibition can trigger a metabolic shift toward lipid storage in Drosophila, and they refute the claim that rapamycin decreases triacylglycerol concentrations in fruit flies.

Recent investigations into the metabolic effects of rapamycin in Drosophila melanogaster have yielded data that directly challenge the hypothesis that rapamycin reduces triacylglycerol (TAG) stores. In a controlled laboratory experiment, adult male and female flies were administered rapamycin at concentrations of 200 µM and 400 µM incorporated into standard corn‑meal medium for a period of 14 days, a regimen previously shown to inhibit TOR signaling without causing overt toxicity. TAG levels were quantified using a colorimetric enzymatic assay normalized to protein content. Contrary to the claim, rapamycin‑treated cohorts displayed a statistically significant increase in whole‑body TAG concentration relative to vehicle‑treated controls (p < 0.01). Specifically, flies receiving 200 µM rapamycin exhibited a 23 ± 4 % elevation in TAG, while the 400 µM group showed a 37 ± 5 % rise. Parallel measurements of glycogen and glucose revealed no compensatory changes, indicating that the observed TAG accumulation was not due to altered carbohydrate metabolism. Moreover, quantitative PCR analysis confirmed down‑regulation of the TOR‑responsive gene 4E‑BP and up‑regulation of lipogenic transcription factors SREBP and dFOXO, suggesting that chronic TOR inhibition may derepress lipogenesis pathways in Drosophila. These findings are consistent with earlier reports that rapamycin can promote lipid storage in flies by shifting metabolic flux toward de novo fatty‑acid synthesis. Collectively, the data refute the claim that rapamycin decreases triacylglycerol concentration in fruit flies and instead support a model in which TOR inhibition by rapamycin leads to TAG accumulation.

Recent investigations into the metabolic effects of rapamycin in Drosophila melanogaster have yielded compelling evidence that the drug reduces whole‑body triacylglycerol (TAG) stores. In a controlled feeding experiment, adult male flies were maintained on a standard corn‑meal diet supplemented with 200 µM rapamycin for 14 days, while matched controls received vehicle only. Quantitative lipidomics performed on homogenates using thin‑layer chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry revealed a 38 ± 5 % decrease in TAG concentration in rapamycin‑treated flies relative to controls (p < 0.001, n = 8 biological replicates). This reduction was accompanied by a modest increase in circulating diacylglycerol and free fatty acids, suggesting enhanced lipolysis. Gene‑expression analysis further demonstrated up‑regulation of the lipase bmm (Brummer) and down‑regulation of the lipogenic transcription factor SREBP, consistent with a shift toward catabolic lipid metabolism. Importantly, the effect was abolished in flies bearing a loss‑of‑function mutation in TOR (Target of Rapamycin), confirming that the TAG‑lowering phenotype is mediated through TOR inhibition. Collectively, these data support the claim that rapamycin decreases triacylglycerol concentration in fruit flies.

The fidelity of bacterial two‑component signaling systems is determined not only by the intrinsic specificity of sensor kinases and response regulators but also by the kinetic parameters governing phosphotransfer. Recent kinetic analyses of the EnvZ‑OmpR and PhoQ‑PhoP pathways demonstrate that rapid phosphotransfer rates (k_cat > 10 s⁻¹) are essential for maintaining signaling accuracy under fluctuating environmental conditions. In vitro phosphotransfer assays using stopped‑flow fluorescence revealed that the half‑life of the phosphoryl‑transfer intermediate is <50 ms for cognate pairs, whereas non‑cognate interactions exhibit markedly slower rates (k_cat < 0.5 s⁻¹) and consequently higher levels of cross‑phosphorylation. Mutagenesis of the conserved His‑Asp phosphotransfer interface in EnvZ (H243A) reduced the phosphotransfer rate by 20‑fold and resulted in a 5‑fold increase in erroneous OmpR phosphorylation by the non‑cognate kinase CpxA, as measured by phospho‑specific Western blotting. Moreover, single‑cell fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) imaging in live cells showed that rapid phosphotransfer limits the dwell time of phosphoryl groups on the histidine kinase, thereby reducing the window for promiscuous phosphotransfer to off‑target regulators. Computational modeling of the phosphotransfer network further supports this kinetic proofreading mechanism: simulations predict that a ≥10‑fold increase in phosphotransfer rate lowers the steady‑state probability of non‑cognate phosphotransfer events from 0.12 to <0.01, without compromising signal amplitude. Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that rapid phosphotransfer rates are a primary determinant of fidelity in two‑component systems, acting as a kinetic filter that discriminates against slow, non‑specific phosphotransfer reactions.

Recent kinetic analyses of prototypical histidine kinase–response regulator pairs demonstrate that the rate of phosphotransfer, rather than the intrinsic autophosphorylation speed of the kinase, is the primary determinant of signaling fidelity in two‑component systems. Using stopped‑flow fluorescence spectroscopy, we measured phosphotransfer half‑times (t½) ranging from 30 ms to 2 s for the EnvZ/OmpR, PhoQ/PhoP and CpxA/CpxR systems. Mutagenesis of the conserved H‑box residues in the kinase catalytic domain altered phosphotransfer rates by up to 25‑fold without appreciably changing ATP‑binding affinity or autophosphorylation kinetics. These alterations produced proportional changes in the ratio of phosphorylated to unphosphorylated response regulator under steady‑state conditions, as quantified by quantitative phospho‑Western blotting and mass‑spectrometric phosphopeptide mapping. Importantly, when phosphotransfer rates were slowed below 200 ms, cross‑talk with non‑cognate regulators increased markedly, as evidenced by ectopic activation of the OmpR‑dependent porin promoter in a ΔompR background expressing a phosphotransfer‑deficient EnvZ mutant. Conversely, engineered hyperactive phosphotransfer variants (t½ ≈ 40 ms) displayed enhanced discrimination, maintaining >95 % specificity even in the presence of tenfold excess of competing response regulators. Computational modeling of the kinetic proofreading network further corroborates that rapid phosphotransfer creates a narrow temporal window that limits the opportunity for non‑cognate interactions, thereby enforcing fidelity. Collectively, these data support the claim that rapid phosphotransfer rates are a governing factor in the high specificity of bacterial two‑component signal transduction.

Recent kinetic analyses of the EnvZ/OmpR two‑component system demonstrate that the phosphotransfer step is not the primary determinant of signaling fidelity. Using stopped‑flow fluorescence spectroscopy, we measured the rate constants for phosphotransfer (k_pt) and for the competing dephosphorylation reactions catalyzed by the cognate phosphatase domain. While k_pt for EnvZ→OmpR exceeds 200 s⁻¹, the rate of OmpR~P hydrolysis by EnvZ is comparably rapid (k_h ≈ 150 s⁻¹), resulting in a narrow window for productive phosphotransfer. Mutagenesis of the conserved His‑Asp catalytic dyad in EnvZ, which reduces k_pt by >10‑fold, does not significantly alter the downstream transcriptional output, because the system compensates through increased OmpR~P stability conferred by auxiliary scaffold proteins. Moreover, single‑cell fluorescence‑activated reporter assays reveal that altering the intracellular concentration of the response regulator changes output variance more dramatically than modulating phosphotransfer kinetics. Together, these data indicate that rapid phosphotransfer rates are insufficient to guarantee high fidelity; instead, fidelity emerges from a balance of phosphotransfer, phosphatase activity, and regulator sequestration, challenging the notion that phosphotransfer speed alone governs specificity in two‑component signaling.

Recent kinetic analyses of prototypical two‑component systems (TCS) reveal that the rate of phosphotransfer from the sensor histidine kinase (HK) to its cognate response regulator (RR) is a decisive determinant of signaling fidelity. In vitro phosphotransfer assays with purified EnvZ/OmpR, NarX/NarL and PhoQ/PhoP pairs demonstrate that the forward phosphotransfer rate constants (k₁) span 10⁴–10⁶ M⁻¹ s⁻¹, whereas the reverse dephosphorylation rates (k₋₁) are at least two orders of magnitude slower. Mutagenesis of the conserved His‑Asp phosphotransfer interface that reduces k₁ by ≈50 % leads to a proportional increase in cross‑talk with non‑cognate RRs, as measured by phosphotransfer to heterologous regulators in competition assays. Conversely, engineered HK variants with accelerated phosphotransfer (k₁ increased 3‑fold) exhibit enhanced specificity, maintaining >95 % phosphotransfer to the intended RR even in the presence of excess alternative RRs. Single‑cell fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) microscopy further corroborates these findings in vivo: cells expressing a fast‑phosphotransfer HK display a sharp, transient pulse of RR phosphorylation that decays rapidly, limiting the temporal window for off‑target interactions. In contrast, slow‑phosphotransfer mutants show prolonged RR phosphorylation tails, during which promiscuous phosphotransfer events become detectable. Together, these data support the claim that rapid phosphotransfer rates are a primary mechanism by which TCS maintain high fidelity, minimizing erroneous signaling through kinetic proofreading of the phosphotransfer step.

Recent investigations into the innate immune response of cerebellar granule cell neurons (GCNs) have demonstrated that the kinetics and magnitude of interferon‑stimulated gene (ISG) expression critically determine neuronal survival following West Nile virus (WNV) infection. In a series of in vitro experiments, primary murine GCN cultures were transduced with lentiviral vectors encoding constitutively active IRF7 or treated with low‑dose recombinant IFN‑β to achieve a modest, sustained up‑regulation of a canonical ISG panel (Mx1, Oas1b, Ifit1, and Isg15). Compared with untreated controls, these pre‑conditioned neurons exhibited a 3.2‑fold increase in basal ISG transcript levels (p < 0.01) and a 4.7‑fold acceleration of ISG induction within the first 6 h post‑infection (p < 0.001). Importantly, the enhanced ISG milieu correlated with a significant reduction in viral replication (peak titers decreased by 78 ± 5 %) and a 65 % increase in neuronal viability at 48 h post‑infection, as measured by calcein‑AM staining and lactate dehydrogenase release assays. Conversely, CRISPR‑Cas9–mediated knockout of the ISG15 locus in GCNs abolished the protective effect, resulting in viral loads comparable to naïve cells and a 30 % decline in survival (p < 0.05). Parallel in vivo studies using conditional IRF7 overexpression in cerebellar granule cells of adult mice confirmed these findings: transgenic mice displayed a 2.8‑fold elevation in basal ISG expression, reduced WNV neuroinvasion, and a 48 % improvement in survival relative to wild‑type littermates (log‑rank p = 0.004). Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that rapid up‑regulation and higher basal expression of interferon‑induced genes confer a neuroprotective advantage to granule cell neurons during WNV infection.

Recent investigations into the neurotropic pathology of West Nile virus (WNV) have revealed a pivotal role for interferon‑stimulated genes (ISGs) in modulating granule cell neuron (GCN) survival. In a series of in vitro experiments using primary murine cerebellar granule cell cultures, rapid up‑regulation of ISGs such as **Mx1**, **Oas1a**, **Ifit1**, and **Irf7** was observed within 2 h post‑infection, preceding detectable viral replication. Quantitative PCR demonstrated a 4‑ to 8‑fold increase in basal ISG transcript levels in GCNs derived from IFNAR1‑heterozygous mice compared with wild‑type controls, correlating with a 60 % reduction in viral titers at 24 h post‑infection (p < 0.01). Moreover, CRISPR‑mediated knockdown of **Mx1** or **Ifit1** abolished the protective effect, resulting in a 2‑fold increase in caspase‑3 activation and a 45 % decrease in neuronal viability (Annexin V/PI assay, p < 0.001). In vivo, transgenic mice engineered to overexpress **Oas1a** under the granule‑cell‑specific GABRA6 promoter exhibited a 70 % survival advantage after peripheral WNV challenge, accompanied by markedly lower viral RNA loads in the cerebellum (RT‑qPCR, ΔCt = 5.2, p < 0.005). Conversely, mice lacking basal ISG expression (IFNAR1‑null) displayed extensive granule cell loss and severe ataxia, underscoring the necessity of pre‑existing ISG expression for neuroprotection. Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that both rapid induction and elevated basal expression of interferon‑induced genes critically enhance the survival of granule cell neurons infected by West Nile virus.

Recent investigations into the innate immune response of cerebellar granule cell neurons (GCNs) to West Nile virus (WNV) infection have demonstrated that the kinetics and magnitude of interferon‑stimulated gene (ISG) expression critically determine neuronal survival. In a comparative transcriptomic analysis of primary murine GCN cultures derived from wild‑type and IFNAR1‑deficient mice, WNV infection induced a rapid up‑regulation of a core ISG signature—including Mx1, Oas1a, Ifit1, Ifit3, Isg15, and Rsad2—within 4 h post‑infection in wild‑type neurons, whereas IFNAR1‑null neurons exhibited delayed and attenuated ISG induction (peak at 12 h, <30 % of wild‑type levels). Correspondingly, basal expression of these ISGs was 2‑ to 3‑fold higher in uninfected wild‑type GCNs relative to IFNAR1‑deficient controls, as quantified by RNA‑seq (FPKM ≈ 12–18 vs. 4–6). Functional assays revealed that pharmacologic augmentation of basal ISG expression using low‑dose recombinant IFN‑β (10 U ml⁻¹) prior to viral challenge increased neuronal viability by 45 % (p < 0.01) and reduced viral titers by 1.8 log₁₀ PFU ml⁻¹ at 24 h post‑infection. Conversely, CRISPR‑mediated knock‑down of Mx1 or Oas1a in wild‑type GCNs abolished the protective effect of early IFN‑β pretreatment, leading to apoptosis rates comparable to IFNAR1‑null cells. These data indicate that both a heightened basal ISG repertoire and a swift transcriptional surge upon WNV exposure are necessary and sufficient to confer resistance to viral cytopathicity in granule cell neurons. Thus, the claim that rapid up‑regulation and higher basal expression of interferon‑induced genes increase survival of WNV‑infected granule cell neurons is strongly supported.

Recent investigations into the innate immune response of cerebellar granule cell neurons (GCNs) have demonstrated that the kinetics and magnitude of interferon-stimulated gene (ISG) expression critically influence neuronal survival following West Nile virus (WNV) infection. In a series of in vitro experiments using primary murine GCN cultures, rapid up‑regulation of a core ISG panel—including Mx1, Oas1b, Ifit1, and Isg15—was observed within 4 h post‑infection in neurons derived from wild‑type mice, whereas neurons from Ifnar1‑deficient mice showed delayed ISG induction (>12 h) and markedly reduced survival (p < 0.001). Quantitative PCR and single‑cell RNA‑seq analyses revealed that basal transcription levels of these ISGs were 2–3‑fold higher in wild‑type GCNs compared with cortical neurons, correlating with a 45 % increase in cell viability at 48 h post‑infection. Pharmacological augmentation of basal ISG expression using low‑dose type I interferon pretreatment further enhanced neuronal survival by 30 % (p = 0.004), whereas siRNA‑mediated knockdown of Mx1 or Oas1b abolished this protective effect, leading to apoptosis rates comparable to untreated controls. In vivo, conditional knockout of Mx1 in granule cells resulted in a 2.5‑fold increase in viral load and a 60 % reduction in cerebellar granule cell layer thickness at day 7 post‑infection, confirming the necessity of rapid ISG activation for neuroprotection. Collectively, these data support the claim that both a higher basal expression of interferon‑induced genes and their swift up‑regulation upon WNV challenge are essential determinants of granule cell neuron survival.

Recent investigations into the innate immune response of cerebellar granule cell neurons (GCNs) to West Nile virus (WNV) infection have revealed a paradoxical relationship between interferon‑stimulated gene (ISG) expression and neuronal survival. In a series of in vitro experiments, primary mouse GCN cultures were transduced with lentiviral vectors encoding constitutively active IRF7 or treated with high‑dose recombinant IFN‑β to achieve rapid up‑regulation and elevated basal levels of a canonical ISG panel (Mx1, Oas1a, Ifit1, and Rsad2). Quantitative RT‑PCR confirmed a 5‑ to 12‑fold increase in ISG transcripts within 4 h post‑treatment, persisting throughout the 72‑h observation period. Upon challenge with a neurovirulent WNV strain (NY99), neurons with pre‑induced ISG expression exhibited a statistically significant reduction in survival (median viability 38 % ± 4 % at 48 h post‑infection) compared with control neurons (median viability 71 % ± 3 %; p < 0.001, log‑rank test). Flow cytometric analysis demonstrated heightened activation of caspase‑3/7 and increased Annexin V binding in the ISG‑overexpressing cohort, indicating an acceleration of apoptotic pathways. Parallel RNA‑seq profiling identified up‑regulation of pro‑apoptotic mediators (Bax, Puma) and down‑regulation of neuroprotective factors (Bcl‑2, Nrf2) uniquely in the high‑ISG condition, suggesting that excessive interferon signaling skews the balance toward cell death. Moreover, pharmacological inhibition of JAK‑STAT signaling with ruxolitinib restored neuronal viability to near‑baseline levels (68 % ± 5 % survival), further implicating the interferon cascade as the driver of the observed toxicity. Collectively, these data support the claim that rapid up‑regulation and higher basal expression of interferon‑induced genes diminish the survival of granule cell neurons infected by West Nile virus, likely by amplifying intrinsic apoptotic mechanisms rather than conferring antiviral protection.

Recent investigations into the neurotropic pathology of West Nile virus (WNV) have revealed a paradoxical role for interferon‑stimulated genes (ISGs) in cerebellar granule cell neurons (GCNs). In a series of in vitro infection experiments, primary murine GCN cultures were transduced with lentiviral vectors encoding constitutively active IRF7, resulting in a three‑fold increase in basal ISG transcription (including Mx1, Oas1b, and Ifit1) compared with unmodified controls (p < 0.01). Upon exposure to a neurovirulent WNV strain (NY99), the IRF7‑overexpressing neurons displayed a significantly higher rate of apoptosis, as measured by Annexin V/propidium iodide staining (45 % ± 3 % versus 22 % ± 2 % in controls at 48 h post‑infection, p < 0.001). Parallel RNA‑seq analyses demonstrated that rapid up‑regulation of ISGs in the first 6 h post‑infection was accompanied by sustained activation of the JAK/STAT pathway and elevated expression of pro‑apoptotic mediators such as Bim and Caspase‑8. Pharmacological blockade of JAK1/2 with ruxolitinib attenuated ISG induction and rescued neuronal viability by ~30 % without compromising viral clearance, indicating that excessive interferon signaling is deleterious in this context. Conversely, knockdown of Mx1 or Oas1b using siRNA reduced early ISG spikes and improved survival of infected GCNs (survival 58 % ± 4 % vs. 32 % ± 3 % in scrambled siRNA controls, p < 0.005), albeit at the cost of higher extracellular viral titers. These data collectively support the claim that both rapid up‑regulation and higher basal expression of interferon‑induced genes exacerbate neuronal death during WNV infection, likely through hyperactivation of downstream apoptotic pathways rather than direct antiviral efficacy.

Recent investigations into the neurotropic pathogenesis of West Nile virus (WNV) have revealed a paradoxical role for type‑I interferon (IFN) signaling within cerebellar granule cell neurons (GCNs). In a series of in‑vitro and in‑vivo experiments, we compared the survival of GCNs derived from wild‑type C57BL/6 mice with that of neurons from transgenic lines engineered to overexpress IFN‑stimulated genes (ISGs) at basal levels. Quantitative PCR demonstrated that basal transcripts of Mx1, Oas1b, and Ifit1 were 3‑ to 7‑fold higher in the transgenic GCNs (p < 0.001). Upon WNV infection (MOI = 0.5), these neurons exhibited a rapid up‑regulation of the same ISGs, reaching peak expression within 6 h post‑infection, whereas wild‑type cells showed a delayed response, with maximal induction at 12–18 h. Despite the accelerated antiviral transcriptional program, live‑cell imaging and flow cytometry indicated a statistically significant reduction in neuronal viability in the high‑ISG cohort: at 48 h post‑infection, only 42 ± 5 % of transgenic GCNs remained viable compared with 71 ± 4 % of wild‑type cells (p = 0.002). Immunohistochemical analysis of cerebellar sections from infected transgenic mice corroborated these findings, showing increased cleaved‑caspase‑3 staining and reduced NeuN‑positive granule cell layers relative to controls. Mechanistically, RNA‑seq profiling revealed that premature ISG activation suppressed the expression of neuroprotective factors such as Bdnf and Nrf2, while concurrently up‑regulating pro‑apoptotic mediators (Bax, Puma). These data collectively refute the notion that heightened basal and rapidly induced interferon‑induced gene expression confers protection; instead, they support the claim that such a response exacerbates neuronal death in granule cell populations infected by WNV.

Recent investigations into the neurotropic pathology of West Nile virus (WNV) have revealed a paradoxical role for interferon‑stimulated genes (ISGs) in cerebellar granule cell neurons (GCNs). In a series of in vitro infections using primary murine GCN cultures, rapid up‑regulation of canonical ISGs—including Ifit1, Mx1, Oas1a, and Isg15—was observed within 4 h post‑infection, reaching peak transcriptional levels two‑fold higher than those measured in cortical neurons under identical conditions. Concomitantly, basal expression of the same ISG panel, assessed in uninfected GCNs from interferon‑α/β receptor‑deficient (Ifnar1⁻/⁻) versus wild‑type littermates, was significantly elevated (p < 0.01), suggesting an intrinsically heightened antiviral tone in granule cells. Despite this robust ISG response, cell‑death assays demonstrated a marked decrease in GCN viability: lactate dehydrogenase release and caspase‑3 activation were 45 % and 3.2‑fold greater, respectively, in wild‑type GCNs compared with Ifnar1⁻/⁻ counterparts at 24 h post‑WNV infection (MOI = 1). Pharmacological blockade of JAK‑STAT signaling with ruxolitinib attenuated ISG induction and rescued neuronal survival by ~30 % (p < 0.05), whereas overexpression of a constitutively active IRF7 construct further amplified ISG transcription and exacerbated cell loss. Transcriptomic profiling of surviving neurons revealed enrichment of pro‑apoptotic pathways (e.g., Bax, Casp8) and suppression of neuroprotective genes (e.g., Bcl‑2, Nrf2) in the high‑ISG cohort. Collectively, these data support the claim that both rapid up‑regulation and elevated basal expression of interferon‑induced genes paradoxically reduce the survival of granule cell neurons infected by West Nile virus, likely through maladaptive activation of intrinsic apoptotic mechanisms rather than effective viral clearance.

Recent high‑resolution chromatin interaction maps generated from 1,200 tumor genomes across ten cancer types reveal that CTCF‑mediated loop anchors are hotspots for somatic alterations. By intersecting the coordinates of CTCF binding motifs (as defined by ENCODE ChIP‑seq peaks) with the Catalogue Of Somatic Mutations In Cancer (COSMIC) dataset, we identified 3,487 recurrent single‑nucleotide variants (SNVs) and 212 small insertions/deletions (indels) that occur in ≥5 independent tumors. Strikingly, 68 % of these events localize within 200 bp of CTCF anchor sites that flank oncogenes such as MYC, CCND1, and EGFR. The mutation frequency at these CTCF anchors (mean = 1.9 × 10⁻⁴ mutations per base) exceeds that of matched genomic background (mean = 5.2 × 10⁻⁵, p < 1 × 10⁻⁶, Fisher’s exact test) and is comparable to the rate observed at known cancer driver loci. Moreover, allele‑specific Hi‑C in cell lines harboring the recurrent CTCF‑anchor mutations demonstrates a loss of loop insulation and ectopic enhancer‑promoter contacts that up‑regulate the adjacent oncogene (fold‑change = 2.3 ± 0.4, q < 0.01). These findings collectively support the claim that recurrent mutations occur frequently within CTCF anchor sites adjacent to oncogenes, implicating disruption of three‑dimensional genome architecture as a recurrent mechanism of oncogene activation.

Recent whole‑genome sequencing analyses of 3,200 tumor specimens across 12 cancer types reveal that recurrent somatic mutations are markedly enriched at CTCF binding motifs that demarcate topologically associating domain (TAD) boundaries adjacent to oncogenic loci. In a pan‑cancer cohort, 27 % of CTCF anchor sites within 50 kb of known driver genes harbored at least one non‑synonymous point mutation, a frequency that exceeds the genome‑wide background rate by 4.8‑fold (p < 1 × 10⁻⁸, Fisher’s exact test). Moreover, mutation density peaks precisely at the core CTCF consensus sequence (CCGCGNGGGC) and is driven largely by C > T transitions at CpG dinucleotides, consistent with APOBEC and age‑related mutational processes. Functional interrogation using CRISPR‑mediated base editing of hotspot mutations at the MYC‑adjacent CTCF site in colorectal cancer organoids results in loss of CTCF occupancy (ChIP‑seq signal reduced by 73 %) and concomitant expansion of the MYC TAD, leading to a 3.2‑fold increase in MYC transcription (RNA‑seq, FDR < 0.01). Similar perturbations at the EGFR and KRAS loci produce comparable derepression of oncogene expression and enhanced proliferative capacity in vitro. Collectively, these data demonstrate that recurrent mutations occur frequently within CTCF anchor sites flanking oncogenes and that such alterations can remodel chromatin architecture to facilitate oncogene activation.

Recent analyses of whole‑genome sequencing data from >2,500 tumor specimens across 30 cancer types reveal that recurrent somatic mutations are significantly enriched at CTCF binding motifs that demarcate chromatin loop anchors proximal to oncogenes. Using high‑resolution Hi‑C maps, we identified 1,842 CTCF‑anchored loops whose anchors lie within 50 kb of known driver genes (e.g., MYC, EGFR, KRAS). Mutational density at these anchors was 3.7‑fold higher than in matched flanking regions (p < 1 × 10⁻⁶, binomial test) after correcting for local replication timing and chromatin accessibility. Moreover, the majority of the recurrent variants (≈68 %) disrupt the core CTCF consensus (CCCTC) and abrogate in vitro binding in electrophoretic‑mobility shift assays. CRISPR‑mediated introduction of representative anchor‑site mutations in breast cancer cell lines leads to loss of CTCF occupancy, rewiring of topologically associating domains, and a 2.5‑fold increase in oncogene transcription (RNA‑seq, DESeq2, FDR < 0.01). These findings collectively demonstrate that recurrent mutations frequently target CTCF anchor sites adjacent to oncogenes, implicating disruption of insulator function as a recurrent mechanism of oncogenic activation.

Recent integrative analyses of whole‑genome sequencing data from >3,000 tumor samples across 30 cancer types reveal a statistically significant enrichment of somatic point mutations within CTCF binding motifs that demarcate chromatin loop anchors proximal to known oncogenes. By intersecting high‑resolution Hi‑C maps with ENCODE CTCF ChIP‑seq peaks, we identified 1,842 loop anchors located within 50 kb of oncogenic loci such as MYC, ERBB2, and CCND1. Mutational burden at these anchors (mean = 4.7 mut/Mb) exceeds that of flanking non‑anchor CTCF sites (mean = 1.9 mut/Mb; p < 1 × 10⁻⁸, Poisson regression) and the genome‑wide background (mean = 1.3 mut/Mb). The excess is driven primarily by recurrent C>T transitions at CpG dinucleotides within the core CTCF consensus (CCGCGNGGNG). Moreover, functional assays demonstrate that CRISPR‑mediated disruption of frequently mutated CTCF motifs at the MYC‑enhancer loop reduces CTCF occupancy, attenuates loop formation (as measured by 4C‑seq), and leads to a 2.3‑fold increase in MYC transcription. Collectively, these data support the claim that recurrent mutations occur frequently within CTCF anchor sites adjacent to oncogenes, suggesting that mutational targeting of architectural proteins contributes to oncogenic deregulation.

Recent investigations have examined the functional relationship between interleukin‑2 (IL‑2) signaling capacity in CD4⁺CD25⁺FOXP3⁺ regulatory T cells (Tregs) and susceptibility to autoimmune pathology, particularly type‑1 diabetes (T1D). In a cohort of non‑obese diabetic (NOD) mice, we observed that Tregs isolated from animals genetically engineered to express a hypomorphic IL‑2Rβ allele (Il2rb^hyp/hyp) displayed a ∼40 % reduction in STAT5 phosphorylation in response to graded concentrations of recombinant IL‑2 compared with wild‑type controls (p < 0.01). Paradoxically, these IL‑2‑hyporesponsive Tregs exhibited enhanced suppressive activity in vitro, as measured by their ability to inhibit CD8⁺ T‑cell proliferation (IC₅₀ = 0.8 µg ml⁻¹ versus 2.3 µg ml⁻¹ for wild‑type Tregs, p < 0.05). In vivo, Il2rb^hyp/hyp NOD mice showed a delayed onset of hyperglycemia (median onset 28 weeks versus 14 weeks in wild‑type NOD, log‑rank test p = 0.003) and a 65 % reduction in insulitis severity (insulitis score 1.2 ± 0.3 versus 3.4 ± 0.5, p < 0.001). Flow cytometric analysis of pancreatic lymph nodes revealed an increased proportion of Helios⁺ Tregs (28 % ± 2 % versus 15 % ± 1 % in controls) and a concomitant decrease in IFN‑γ‑producing CD4⁺ Th1 cells (4.3 % ± 0.5 % versus 9.8 % ± 0.7 %, p < 0.01). Transcriptomic profiling of the hyporesponsive Tregs identified up‑regulation of genes associated with metabolic fitness (e.g., Cpt1a, Glut1) and the suppressive effector program (e.g., Ctla4, Il10), while genes linked to IL‑2‑driven proliferation (e.g., Myc, Cyclin D2) were down‑regulated. Collectively, these data demonstrate that a calibrated reduction in IL‑2 responsiveness endows Tregs with a phenotype that is both metabolically resilient and functionally suppressive, thereby conferring increased resistance to the development of T1D. This challenges the prevailing view that maximal IL‑2 signaling is universally beneficial for Treg‑mediated tolerance and suggests that therapeutic modulation of IL‑2 sensitivity could be exploited to enhance autoimmune protection.

Recent investigations into the cytokine signaling pathways of CD4⁺CD25⁺FOXP3⁺ regulatory T cells (Tregs) have revealed a paradoxical relationship between interleukin‑2 (IL‑2) responsiveness and susceptibility to autoimmune pathology. Using a combination of phospho‑STAT5 flow cytometry, quantitative PCR for IL‑2Rα (CD25) transcription, and in vivo disease models, we demonstrated that Tregs derived from non‑obese diabetic (NOD) mice exhibit a markedly attenuated response to exogenous IL‑2, as evidenced by a 45 ± 7 % reduction in STAT5 phosphorylation relative to Tregs from C57BL/6 controls (p < 0.01). This hyporesponsiveness correlates with a sustained expression of the inhibitory phosphatase SHP‑2 and increased methylation of the IL2RA promoter, which together diminish downstream signaling despite normal surface CD25 density.

Functionally, the IL‑2‑hyporesponsive Tregs retain superior suppressive capacity in vitro, inhibiting effector T‑cell proliferation at a 1:1 ratio more effectively than their IL‑2‑responsive counterparts (IC₅₀ = 0.8 ng mL⁻¹ vs. 2.3 ng mL⁻¹, p < 0.05). In adoptive transfer experiments, NOD‑derived Tregs conferred a 62 % reduction in the incidence of hyperglycemia in recipient NOD recipients (p = 0.004), whereas Tregs pre‑treated with low‑dose IL‑2 lost this protective effect. Moreover, pharmacologic blockade of the IL‑2 receptor in wild‑type mice recapitulated the protective phenotype, with a 48 % decrease in insulitis scores (p < 0.01) and preservation of β‑cell mass over a 12‑week observation period.

Collectively, these data refute the conventional view that heightened IL‑2 signaling uniformly benefits Treg function. Instead, they support the claim that a calibrated reduction in IL‑2 responsiveness endows Tregs with enhanced stability and suppressive potency, thereby conferring greater resistance to autoimmune diseases such as Type 1 Diabetes.

Recent investigations into the cytokine signaling pathways of CD4⁺CD25⁺FOXP3⁺ regulatory T cells (Tregs) have revealed a paradoxical relationship between interleukin‑2 (IL‑2) responsiveness and susceptibility to autoimmune pathology. In a cohort of non‑obese diabetic (NOD) mice, Tregs isolated from animals that remained normoglycemic after 30 weeks displayed markedly attenuated phosphorylation of STAT5 in response to graded concentrations of recombinant IL‑2, compared with Tregs from mice that progressed to overt Type 1 diabetes (T1D) (p < 0.01). This hyporesponsive phenotype was accompanied by up‑regulation of the IL‑2Rβ chain (CD122) and the phosphatase SHP‑2, suggesting a compensatory down‑modulation of downstream signaling rather than receptor deficiency. Functionally, these IL‑2‑hyporesponsive Tregs exhibited enhanced suppressive capacity in vitro, as measured by a >2‑fold reduction in proliferation of autologous CD8⁺ effector T cells (CFSE dilution assay, p < 0.001), and they maintained stable FOXP3 expression under inflammatory conditions (IL‑6 + TNF‑α). Adoptive transfer of IL‑2‑hyporesponsive Tregs into pre‑diabetic NOD recipients delayed onset of hyperglycemia by a median of 12 weeks (log‑rank test, p = 0.004). Conversely, pharmacologic augmentation of IL‑2 signaling using low‑dose IL‑2 complexes increased STAT5 activation in Tregs but paradoxically diminished their suppressive function and accelerated β‑cell loss in the same model. Human peripheral blood samples corroborated these findings: individuals with a first‑degree relative with T1D who remained seronegative for islet autoantibodies for >5 years showed reduced IL‑2‑induced pSTAT5 in Tregs (mean ± SD: 18 ± 4 % versus 31 ± 5 % in autoantibody‑positive relatives, p = 0.002) and higher expression of the inhibitory receptor LAG‑3. Collectively, these data support the claim that a diminished IL‑2 responsiveness in Tregs is associated with increased resistance to autoimmune diabetes, likely through the preservation of a highly suppressive, phenotypically stable Treg compartment that limits autoreactive effector activation.

Recent investigations have examined the functional relationship between interleukin‑2 (IL‑2) signaling and the suppressive capacity of CD4⁺CD25⁺FOXP3⁺ regulatory T cells (Tregs) in the context of autoimmune diabetes. Using the non‑obese diabetic (NOD) mouse model, we compared Tregs isolated from disease‑prone NOD mice with those from NOD mice genetically engineered to express a hypomorphic IL‑2 receptor β chain (Il2rb^hypo), which reduces IL‑2–mediated STAT5 phosphorylation by ~40 % relative to wild‑type controls. Flow cytometric analysis demonstrated that Il2rb^hypo Tregs exhibited markedly lower surface CD25 expression and diminished pSTAT5 responses upon ex vivo IL‑2 stimulation (p < 0.01). Despite this attenuated signaling, the hypomorphic Tregs maintained expression of key suppressive molecules (CTLA‑4, LAG‑3, and IL‑10) at levels comparable to wild‑type Tregs. In longitudinal studies, Il2rb^hypo NOD mice displayed a significant delay in insulitis onset and a 55 % reduction in cumulative diabetes incidence by 30 weeks of age (log‑rank p = 0.003). Adoptive transfer experiments further revealed that Il2rb^hypo Tregs, when co‑administered with diabetogenic CD8⁺ T cells, conferred superior protection against β‑cell destruction compared with wild‑type Tregs (p = 0.02). Mechanistically, reduced IL‑2 responsiveness limited the proliferation of autoreactive effector T cells without compromising Treg‑mediated suppression, thereby creating a functional imbalance that favors tolerance. These data refute the notion that heightened IL‑2 sensitivity is uniformly beneficial for autoimmunity control and instead support the claim that a calibrated decrease in IL‑2 responsiveness in Tregs is associated with increased resistance to Type 1 Diabetes.

Recent chromatin‑immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP‑seq) and nascent‑RNA profiling in *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* reveal that genome‑wide incorporation of the H2A variant H2A.Z (encoded by *HTZ1*) preferentially occupies the +1 nucleosome downstream of transcription start sites (TSSs). Quantitative nucleosome‑turnover assays using histone‑exchange reporters demonstrate that H2A.Z‑containing +1 nucleosomes exhibit a ∼2‑fold longer residence time than canonical H2A‑containing nucleosomes (half‑life ≈ 12 min versus 6 min). In parallel, kinetic measurements of transcription induction after galactose addition to *GAL1* and *GAL10* promoters show a delayed onset of RNA polymerase II recruitment in *HTZ1*‑overexpressing strains (Δt ≈ 5 min) relative to wild‑type cells, whereas *htz1Δ* mutants display accelerated activation (Δt ≈ 2 min). Importantly, mutating the H2A.Z acidic patch to mimic H2A restores nucleosome turnover rates and rescues the activation delay, indicating that the stabilizing effect is intrinsic to the H2A.Z protein. Together, these data support the claim that replacement of canonical H2A by H2A.Z stabilizes the +1 nucleosome and consequently slows the kinetics of gene activation in yeast.

Recent genome‑wide nucleosome mapping in *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* demonstrates that incorporation of the H2A variant H2A.Z into the +1 nucleosome markedly delays transcriptional induction of stress‑responsive genes. Using ChIP‑seq for H2A.Z and RNA polymerase II (Pol II) after heat shock, we observed that genes whose promoters are enriched for H2A.Z exhibit a 3–5‑minute lag in Pol II recruitment relative to H2A‑only promoters, despite comparable upstream activator binding. MNase digestion profiles further reveal that H2A.Z‑containing +1 nucleosomes display reduced DNA accessibility and increased resistance to remodeling by the SWI/SNF complex in vitro. Mutational replacement of the H2A.Z docking surface (ΔN‑tail) restores nucleosome turnover rates to wild‑type H2A levels and abolishes the activation delay, confirming a causal role for H2A.Z in stabilizing the +1 nucleosome. Together, these data support the hypothesis that replacement of canonical H2A with H2A.Z slows gene activation in yeast by enhancing the structural stability of the +1 nucleosome and impeding rapid nucleosome eviction during transcriptional onset.

Recent chromatin‑immunoprecipitation coupled with high‑resolution MNase‑seq in Saccharomyces cerevisiae demonstrates that incorporation of the H2A.Z variant into nucleosomes flanking transcription start sites markedly stabilizes the +1 nucleosome and delays the onset of transcriptional activation. In wild‑type cells, promoters that acquire H2A.Z show a ∼30 % increase in nucleosome occupancy at the +1 position relative to promoters containing canonical H2A, and the residence time of RNA polymerase II at these promoters is extended by 2–3 minutes after induction with galactose. Conversely, deletion of the HTZ1 gene (encoding H2A.Z) or mutation of the Swr1‑dependent deposition complex results in a more labile +1 nucleosome, reduced nucleosomal barrier, and a ∼40 % acceleration of gene induction kinetics. These findings are consistent with a model in which H2A.Z‑containing nucleosomes form a more stable, less dynamic barrier at the +1 position, thereby slowing the recruitment and clearance of the transcriptional machinery and ultimately retarding gene activation in yeast.

Recent chromatin‑immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP‑seq) analyses in *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* have shown that incorporation of the H2A variant H2A.Z (encoded by *HTZ1*) preferentially occurs at nucleosomes flanking the transcription start site, particularly the +1 nucleosome (Kobor et al., 2022). Genome‑wide nucleosome‑positioning maps generated by MNase‑seq in wild‑type versus *htz1Δ* strains reveal that loss of H2A.Z leads to a marked decrease in nucleosome occupancy and an increase in nucleosome turnover at the +1 position (Zhang et al., 2023). Conversely, re‑introduction of H2A.Z restores a more stable +1 nucleosome, as measured by reduced histone exchange rates using a histone‑H3‑FLAG pulse‑chase assay (Liu et al., 2024). Functional assays further demonstrate that genes with H2A.Z‑enriched +1 nucleosomes exhibit delayed induction kinetics after heat‑shock or galactose addition, as quantified by real‑time PCR of nascent transcripts (average lag time 6.2 ± 0.8 min) compared with genes lacking H2A.Z at their +1 nucleosome (lag time 3.1 ± 0.5 min; p < 0.001). In contrast, *htz1Δ* cells display accelerated activation of the same gene set (average lag time 2.4 ± 0.4 min). These findings are consistent with a model in which H2A.Z incorporation stabilizes the +1 nucleosome, creating a kinetic barrier that must be overcome by chromatin remodelers before RNA polymerase II can engage the promoter. Thus, the replacement of canonical H2A with H2A.Z indeed slows gene activation in yeast by stabilizing the +1 nucleosome.

Ribosomopathies, despite arising from mutations in universally expressed ribosomal proteins or biogenesis factors, frequently manifest with strikingly tissue‑restricted phenotypes, contradicting the notion that they exhibit a low degree of cell and tissue specificity. Clinical observations across multiple ribosomopathies illustrate this paradox. Diamond‑Blackfan anemia (DBA) is characterized predominantly by erythroid failure, with patients presenting macrocytic anemia and reticulocytopenia while most other hematopoietic lineages remain relatively intact (Mason & He, 2015). Similarly, Shwachman‑Diamond syndrome (SDS) primarily affects the exocrine pancreas and neutrophil compartment, leading to pancreatic insufficiency and neutropenia, yet sparing other organ systems (Giri et al., 2019). In contrast, cartilage‑hair hypoplasia (CHH) displays severe skeletal dysplasia and immunodeficiency, whereas other tissues are less affected (Al-Mousa et al., 2020). Even within the same organism, murine models harboring hypomorphic alleles of the ribosomal protein Rps19 recapitulate the erythroid bias observed in DBA, whereas Rpl24 mutants preferentially disrupt intestinal epithelium homeostasis (McGowan et al., 2021). These examples underscore that the pathological impact of ribosomal defects is highly context‑dependent, reflecting differential sensitivities of proliferative or highly translationally active cell types to ribosome insufficiency. Mechanistically, tissue specificity can be attributed to several factors: (i) variable expression levels of the mutated ribosomal component across lineages, (ii) distinct translational programs that rely on specialized ribosome subpopulations (ribosome heterogeneity), and (iii) activation of p53‑dependent nucleolar stress pathways that are differentially calibrated in each cell type (Fancello et al., 2022). Consequently, the empirical evidence from both human patients and animal models refutes the claim that ribosomopathies have a low degree of cell and tissue specific pathology; rather, they constitute a paradigm of globally expressed genetic lesions producing highly selective clinical manifestations.

Ribosomopathies, despite originating from mutations in universally expressed ribosomal proteins or biogenesis factors, frequently manifest with strikingly tissue‑restricted phenotypes, contradicting the notion that they exhibit a low degree of cell‑ and tissue‑specific pathology. Comparative analyses of patient cohorts and animal models reveal that the clinical spectrum of ribosomopathies is dominated by defects in hematopoietic lineages, craniofacial structures, and the skeletal system. For example, Diamond‑Blackfan anemia (DBA) is caused by haploinsufficiency of ribosomal proteins RPS19, RPL5, or RPL11 and presents almost exclusively as a red‑cell aplasia, yet spares other lineages (Mason & Horowitz, 2020). Likewise, mutations in the small‑subunit biogenesis factor SBDS underlie Shwachman‑Diamond syndrome, whose hallmark features are exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and neutropenia, while most other tissues retain normal function (Ciccone et al., 2022). In the case of cartilage‑hair hypoplasia, loss‑of‑function variants in the RNA‑polymerase III subunit RMRP produce severe skeletal dysplasia and immunodeficiency, with minimal impact on hepatic or renal physiology (Wang et al., 2021).
